title: Critical Access: Where to Place the Control?
context: An administrator must access a critical server from outside the network. You must design the access path and decide the behavior if the control fails.

n1.text: Which first check must be required before granting access?

choices.text: Authenticate the user (MFA) and verify device health/inventory
choices.why: Zero Trust verifies identity and device before any access, even from outside.

choices.text: Accept the connection if it comes from a known IP
choices.why: Network location is not proof of identity in Zero Trust.
A password alone covers neither device health nor least privilege.

n2.text: Which path should administration go through?

choices.text: A jump host/bastion on an out-of-band network, with MFA and recorded sessions
choices.why: The bastion enforces a single, tracked entry point separated from the user network.

choices.text: Directly via RDP from the administrator's workstation
choices.why: Direct access bypasses centralized control and logging.
This is not a controlled administration channel.

n3.text: The authentication service goes down during the maintenance. Which failure mode should you choose for this critical server?

choices.text: Fail-closed: block access as long as authentication is unavailable
choices.why: For a critical server, denying unauthenticated access takes precedence over continuity.

choices.text: Fail-open: allow traffic through so maintenance is not interrupted
choices.why: Fail-open would allow unverified access to a critical system.
An outage is not a reason to remove traceability.

n4.outcome: You verified identity and device, enforced the out-of-band bastion, and chose fail-closed on a critical asset.

debrief: Zero Trust verifies the user, the device, and application access, not just the network.
The out-of-band bastion centralizes and tracks administration.
Failure mode is decided by criticality: availability or denial of unverified access.
